[^1147]: Fourth and concluding Stasis of the Akathist Hymn (Stanzas 19–24, Greek alphabet Tau through Omega, T–Ω): Ikos 10 (T: Τεῖχος εἶ τῶν παρθένων / Стѣна̀ є҆сѝ дѣ́вамъ) with its twelve angelic salutations invoking the Theotokos as the pillar of virginity, gate of salvation, and guide of divine purity; Kontakion 11 (Y: Ὕμνος ἅπας ἡττᾶται / Пѣ́нїе всѧ́кое побѣжда́етсѧ); Ikos 11 (Ph: Φωτοδόχον λαμπάδα / Свѣтопрїе́мнꙋю свѣщꙋ̀); and Kontakion 12 (Ch: Χάριν δοῦναι θελήσας / Бл҃года́ть да́ти восхотѣ́въ).

[^1148]: Conclusion of the Fourth Stasis of the Akathist Hymn: Ikos 12 (Ps: Ψάλλοντές σου τὸν τόκον / Пою́ще твоѐ ржⷭ҇тво̀), extolling the Mother of God as the living temple, the Holy of Holies, the ark gilded by the Spirit, the unshakeable tower of the Church, and the invincible wall of the realm; and Kontakion 13 (O: Ὦ πανύμνητε Μῆτερ / Ѽ всепѣ́таѧ Мт҃и), chanted thrice, followed by the repetition of Ikos 1 ("An Archangel was sent...") and Kontakion 1 ("To thee, the Champion Leader").

[^1149]: Synaxarion of the Saturday of the Akathist (Praise of the Most Holy Theotokos), commemorating the miraculous divine deliverance of Constantinople from the joint siege of the Persians (under King Khosrow II and his general Shahrbaraz / Sarbaros) and the Avars/Scythians (under the Chagan / Khagan) in 626 AD during the reign of Emperor Heraclius (610–641). While the emperor was campaigning in Persia, Patriarch Sergius I led liturgical processions along the city walls bearing the Icon of Christ Not-Made-by-Hands, the relic of the True Cross, and the Robe (Maphorion) of the Virgin Mary, and Patrician Bonus directed the military defense. A miraculous storm destroyed the enemy fleet at Blachernae in the Golden Horn, prompting the entire populace to maintain an all-night thanksgiving vigil standing upright, giving origin to the title "Akathist" (unseated hymn).

[^1150]: Continuation of the Akathist Synaxarion, documenting subsequent historical deliverances of the Imperial City attributed to the Mother of God: the first Arab siege under Emperor Constantine IV Pogonatus (674–678 AD) with the destruction of the Saracen fleet at Syllaeum, and the second Arab siege under Emperor Leo III the Isaurian (717–718 AD) through the protection of the Holy Cross and the Hodigitria icon, resulting in the destruction of the Muslim fleet by storms and famine. The rubric notes that whereas during other readings the congregation sits, during this thanksgiving office all stand upright.

[^1151]: Ode 7 of the Canon of the Akathist in Tone 4, Heirmos "The godly-minded youths worshipped not creation" (Не послꙋжи́ша тва́ри), with stanzas carrying the Greek acrostic letters Α-Ι-Ρ-Ε-Ι (completing the word χαίρειν, with the final letter Nu following in Ode 8), praising the Virgin Mary as the spiritual chariot of the Sun, the mystical rod blooming with the unfading flower, and the living scroll inscribed by the finger of God the Father.

[^1152]: Second Canon of Ode 7 in Tone 5, Heirmos "Blessed art Thou, O God" (Бл҃гослове́нъ є҆сѝ Бж҃е), with martyrial troparia, Trinitarian doxology, and Theotokion. Opening of Ode 8 of the Canon of the Akathist, Heirmos "The pious youths in the furnace," carrying the Greek acrostic letters Ν (completing χαίρειν), Μ, and Ο (initiating the word μόνῃ).

[^1153]: Conclusion of Ode 8 of the Canon of the Akathist in Tone 4, with stanzas carrying the Greek acrostic letters Ν and Η (completing the word μόνῃ / Μ-Ο-Ν-Η), celebrating the Theotokos as the restoration of the dead, the cleansing of lepers, and the healing of diseases. Followed by the second canon in Tone 6 ("Out of the flame for the venerable...") and third canon in Tone 5 ("The Creator of creation, Whom the Angels dread..."), honoring the holy martyrs and praying for the departed.

[^1154]: Ode 9 of the Canon of the Akathist in Tone 4, Heirmos "Every earthborn mortal" (Всѧ́къ земноро́дный), carrying the final five letters of the Greek acrostic forming the name of the hymnographer: Ι-Ω-Σ-Η-Φ (Ἰωσήφ / Joseph), praising the Theotokos as the unwaning star, the open Eden, the vessel of inexhaustible Myrrh, the pillar of fire, and the immaculate dove. Followed by the second canon in Tone 6 ("God it is impossible for men to see") and third canon in Tone 5 ("Rejoice, O Isaiah").

[^1155]: Exapostilarion of the Saturday of the Akathist, set to the melodic model Podoben "Give ear, ye women" (Γυναῖκες ἀκουτίσθητε / Жены̀ ᲂу҆слы́шите): "The mystery hidden from the ages is made known today..." At the Praises (Lauds), three Prosomoia of the Annunciation doubled to four in Tone 4, set to the melodic model Podoben "As one valiant among martyrs" (Ὡς γενναῖον ἐν μάρτυσιν / Ꙗ҆́кѡ до́блѧ), followed by the festal Doxasticon in Tone 4 ("The Mother of God heard a tongue which she knew not..."), the Great Doxology, and Dismissal.

[^1156]: Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom on the Saturday of the Akathist. At the Beatitudes, troparia from Odes 3 and 6 of the Akathist Canon are appointed. Scriptural pericopes: Prokeimenon in Tone 3, the Magnificat (Luke 1:46–48); Epistle of the day, Hebrews 9:24–28 (Pericope 322); Epistle of the Theotokos, Hebrews 9:1–7 (Pericope 320); Alleluia in Tone 8, Psalm 131:8, 1; Gospel of the day, Mark 8:34–9:1 (Pericope 35); Gospel of the Theotokos, Luke 10:38–42, 11:27–28 (Pericope 54); Communion Hymn, Psalm 115:4 ("I will take the cup of salvation..."). Refectory rule permitting two cooked courses with oil and wine.

[^1157]: Physical leaf p317 = Printed Folio 313 + 4. Iconographic cross-reference: the full-page woodcut plate of the Crucifixion of our Lord Jesus Christ on Golgotha reappears identically at the conclusion of Saturday of the Akathist on folio 406 (physical leaf p410), serving as a visual monument preceding the services of the Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast (Commemoration of our Venerable Mother Mary of Egypt).

[^1158]: Commemoration of our Venerable Mother Mary of Egypt on the Fifth Sunday of the Great Fast. The Slavonic rubric notes the historical layering of the Byzantine rite: the ancient Sabaite and Constantinopolitan Typika appointed only the Resurrectional services of the Octoechos with the Menaion of the calendar date, while the later Studite and neo-Sabaitic synthesis (from the 11th–12th centuries onwards) definitively transferred the commemoration of St. Mary of Egypt (historically celebrated on April 1) to the Fifth Sunday of Lent, alongside the Great Canon sung on the preceding Thursday.

[^1159]: Slavonic: Ѿ чꙋдесѐ но́вагѡ (Greek: Ὢ καινοῦ θαύματος). Sessional/Theotokion of Tone 2, Dogmatikon of the Octoechos.

[^1160]: Liturgical structure of Matins for the Fifth Sunday of Lent: the three canons appointed are (1) the Resurrectional Canon from the Octoechos of the current Tone (with its Theotokion stanzas) counted for 6 troparia; (2) the Triodion Canon on the Rich Man and Lazarus in Tone 8 (composed by St. Theodore the Studite) for 4 troparia; and (3) the Triodion Canon for St. Mary of Egypt in Tone 6 (also attributed to the Studite tradition) for 4 troparia, totaling 14 troparia per ode.

[^1161]: The Lenten Sunday themes in the Studite Triodion are organized typologically: the Fifth Sunday pairs the Gospel parable of the Rich Man and Poor Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31) with the life of St. Mary of Egypt as the archetypal model of radical repentance and ascetic transformation.

[^1162]: Order of the Sunday Matins conclusion: the Great Doxology is sung, followed by the Dismissal Troparion of the Resurrection, the Great Dismissal, the Doxasticon of the Resurrectional Matins Gospel (the Evangelical Sticheron), and the First Hour.

[^1163]: Divine Liturgy of St. Basil the Great on the Fifth Sunday of Lent: the Beatitudes from the Octoechos for 8 troparia. Prokeimenon of the Resurrectional Tone, and for St. Mary of Egypt in Tone 4, Psalm 67:36 ("God is wonderful in His saints").

[^1164]: Scriptural readings for the Fifth Sunday of Lent: Epistle of the Sunday, Hebrews 9:11–14 (Pericope 321 from the midpoint); Epistle of the Venerable Woman, Galatians 3:23–29 (Pericope 208); Gospel of the Sunday, Mark 10:32–45 (Pericope 37, Christ's third prophecy of His Passion and the request of the sons of Zebedee); Gospel of the Venerable Woman, Luke 7:36–50 (Pericope 33, the woman who was a sinner anointing the feet of Jesus in the house of Simon the Pharisee).

[^1165]: Refectory rule for Sunday of Lent: two cooked meals with wine and oil are permitted, with abstention from meat, dairy, eggs, and fish.

[^1166]: The opening sticheron of Sunday evening marks the liturgical transition to the Sixth Week of the Great Fast (Palm Week), introducing the prefestal themes of the Entrance of our Lord into Jerusalem and the raising of Lazarus.

[^1167]: Physical leaf p179 = Printed Folio 175 + 4. Cross-reference to the Great Prokeimenon of Sunday evening in Tone 8: "Thou hast given an inheritance to them that fear Thy name" (Psalm 60:6 LXX), first printed with its verses at Vespers on the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

[^1168]: Monday of the Sixth Week of Lent initiates the solemn cycle of Palm Week (Седми́ца ва́їй / Ἑβδομὰς τῶν βαΐων), directing the Church's contemplation toward the raising of the four-days-dead Lazarus in Bethany and the triumphal entry of the Lord into Jerusalem.

[^1169]: Sessional hymn following the third stichology of the Psalter on Monday of Palm Week. The hymn marks the formal liturgical entry into the Sixth Week of the Great Fast (Седми́ца ва́їй / Ἑβдоμὰς τῶν βαΐων), interweaving the ascetic completion of the Forty Days with the approaching resurrection of Lazarus and the triumphal entry of the Lord into Jerusalem.

[^1170]: The two Matins canons (triodia) of Monday of Palm Week: the first triodion (Odes 1, 8, and 9) in Tone 1 is by St. Joseph the Hymnographer, emphasizing personal compunction, repentance from spiritual sloth, and liberation from the fate of the unmerciful rich man. The second triodion in Tone 1 is by St. Theodore the Studite, dramatizing the impending journey of Christ from beyond Jordan toward Bethany and Bethphage to raise Lazarus.

[^1171]: Ode 8 of the Studite triodion addresses Bethany directly as the honored home of Lazarus, Martha, and Mary, portraying the village as the holy threshold of the Lord's victory over hades and death.

[^1172]: The Aposticha Idiomelon of Monday Matins in Tone 5 takes up the Gospel archetype of the Rich Man and Poor Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), invoking the imagery of the beggar cast before the gate to plead for drops of divine mercy before the dread tribunal.

[^1173]: The Sixth Hour of Monday of Palm Week appoints the Troparion of the Prophecy in Tone 6 ("This is, O God, the fearful day..."), accompanied by two prokeimena from the Psalter (Psalms 104 and 105 LXX) and the prophetic reading from Isaiah 48:17–49:4, which speaks of the redemption of Jacob and introduces the Servant Song of the Messiah called from the maternal womb.

[^1174]: Monday of Palm Week at Vespers: the stichera at "Lord, I have cried" combine St. Joseph's hymn of penitential healing on the bed of slothfulness with St. Theodore's contemplation of Christ walking beyond the Jordan and announcing that the sickness of Lazarus is not unto death, but for the glory of God (John 11:4).

[^1175]: The Old Testament reading at Vespers from Genesis 27:1–41 recounts the patriarchal narrative of Isaac blessing Jacob with the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth, prefiguring the spiritual inheritance granted to the Church from among the Gentiles.

[^1176]: The second reading at Vespers from Proverbs 19:16–25 provides moral exhortations on keeping the divine commandments, showing mercy to the poor as lending unto the Lord, and heeding parental instruction.

[^1177]: Epigraphic defect on physical leaf p427 (printed folio 423) in the concluding Aposticha Theotokion at Monday Vespers. Due to an inking void / printing defect in the Stauropegion edition, words between the left and right fragments are lost: '...го̀ Бг҃а, ро́ждшаѧ всѣ́хъ Творца̀, да всѝ' and 'зове́... хъ на́шихъ.' Restored according to the standard Byzantine-Slavonic Triodion witness: '[И҆зба́ви на́съ ѿ нꙋ́ждъ на́шихъ, Мт҃и Хрⷭ҇та̀] го̀ Бг҃а, ро́ждшаѧ всѣ́хъ Творца̀, да всѝ зове́[мъ тѝ: ра́дꙋйсѧ є҆ди́но предста́тельство дꙋ́ш]хъ на́шихъ.'

[^1178]: Tuesday of Palm Week at Matins: the service continues the prefestal contemplation of Lazarus's sickness and death, appointing penitential sessional hymns from the Octoechos and proper sessional hymns by St. Joseph and St. Theodore.

[^1179]: Appointment of Ode 2 on Tuesday of Palm Week. Outside of the Great Fast, the second biblical ode (the Song of Moses in Deuteronomy 32) is omitted from the daily Matins canon. In the Triodion, Tuesdays retain Ode 2, here paired with triodia by St. Joseph (Tone 6) and St. Theodore (Tone 5).

[^1180]: Ode 9 of Tuesday Matins portrays Lazarus on the brink of physical death ('being about to die tomorrow') and Bethany preparing his tomb, setting the dramatic timeline leading up to Lazarus Saturday.

[^1181]: The Matins Aposticha Idiomelon of Tuesday of Palm Week in Tone 5 combines two biblical warnings against spiritual sloth: Lot fleeing the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah without looking back (Gen. 19:17, 26), and the parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), wherein the beggar is received into Abraham's bosom while the unmerciful rich man burns in torment.

[^1182]: The Sixth Hour on Tuesday of Palm Week appoints the Troparion of the Prophecy in Tone 5 ("An invincible rampart hast Thou given unto our city..."), followed by two prokeimena from the Psalter (Psalms 108 and 109 LXX) and the prophetic reading from Isaiah 49:6–10.

[^1183]: Reading from the Prophecy of Isaiah (49:6–10) at the Sixth Hour of Tuesday: the passage continues the Servant Songs of the Messiah, declaring Christ to be given as a covenant for the people and a light to the Gentiles, establishing the earth and liberating prisoners from spiritual bonds.

[^1184]: The Tuesday Vespers stichera at "Lord, I have cried" in Tone 2 by St. Joseph the Hymnographer allegorize the death of Lazarus into the interior state of the sinner, whose heart lies buried in the tomb of despondency and covered with the stone of insensibility, crying for Christ to awaken it by the Wood of the Cross.

[^1185]: Sticheron by St. Theodore the Studite at Tuesday Vespers in Tone 3 marking the dramatic progression of Palm Week: "Today Lazarus hath breathed his last, and Bethany weeps for him" (Днесь издыше Лазарь), anticipating the Lord's arrival to raise him on Lazarus Saturday.

[^1186]: Reading from Genesis 31:3–16 at Tuesday Vespers: Jacob receives the divine command to depart from Padan-aram and return to Canaan with Leah, Rachel, and his flocks, recounting God's protective intervention against Laban's deceit.

[^1187]: Reading from Proverbs 21:3–21 appointed across Tuesday Vespers (fol. 429–430 / physical leaves p433–p434), contrasting the blessings of righteousness, mercy, and diligent labor with the destruction awaiting deceit and pride.

[^1188]: The Tuesday Vespers Aposticha Idiomelon in Tone 1 contrasts the royal purple robe of dominion and the scarlet mantle of incorruption bestowed upon the soul with the purple robe of mockery placed upon Christ before His crucifixion (Matt. 27:28), calling the Christian to spiritual poverty.

[^1189]: Wednesday of Palm Week at Matins: following the second stichology of the Psalter, the sessional hymn by St. Joseph the Hymnographer in Tone 2 portrays the sinner weighed down by sins as with a grave stone, pleading for Christ to raise him from the tomb of negligence.

[^1190]: Sessional hymn by St. Theodore the Studite following the third stichology on Wednesday Matins in Tone 3: "Today Lazarus, having died, is buried" (Днесь Лазарь умерый погребается), tracking the chronological sequence of the four days in the tomb.

[^1191]: The two Matins canons (triodia) of Wednesday of Palm Week: the first triodion (Odes 3, 8, and 9) in Tone 2 is by St. Joseph the Hymnographer, focused on awakening the mind from the slumber of despondency. The second triodion in Tone 3 is by St. Theodore the Studite, dramatizing Christ's announcement to the disciples that Lazarus is fallen asleep and St. Thomas's courageous resolve to accompany Him into Judea (John 11:16).

[^1192]: Ode 8 of the Studite triodion on Wednesday Matins portrays Lazarus being carried out to the grave ("Today Lazarus, having died, is carried out for burial") while Christ approaches with joy to reveal His divine power as the Life of all.

[^1193]: Ode 9 of the Studite triodion depicts Mary and Martha weeping under the bitter stone of the sepulcher, while Christ declares from afar that He rejoices for the apostles' sakes that He was not there, in order that they may believe (John 11:15).

[^1194]: The Matins Aposticha Idiomelon of Wednesday of Palm Week in Tone 1 offers an allegorical and patristic exposition of the Parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31): Israel, formerly robed in priestly and royal vesture under the Law and the Prophets, now thirsts outside the Kingdom for having rejected the crucified Christ, while the Gentiles, formerly destitute of truth, are now comforted in Abraham's bosom, clothed in the purple of Christ's blood and the scarlet of baptism.

[^1195]: The Sixth Hour on Wednesday of Palm Week appoints the Troparion of the Prophecy in Tone 5 ("Deal Thy mercies with us, O Lord..."), accompanied by two prokeimena from the Psalter (Psalms 112 and 113 LXX) and the prophetic reading from Isaiah 58:1–11.

[^1196]: Reading from the Prophecy of Isaiah (58:1–11) at the Sixth Hour of Wednesday: the definitive prophetic charter on the true fast, rejecting empty ascetic posturing accompanied by contention and oppression, and demanding active works of mercy, the liberation of the bound, and the feeding of the hungry.

[^1197]: Wednesday of Palm Week at Vespers: the idiomelon at "Lord, I have cried" in Tone 5 resumes the theme of Dives and Lazarus, imploring Christ to grant the speaker the poverty in sins of Lazarus (Лазара мя сотвори, нищаго грѣхами) rather than the fiery torment of the heartless rich man.

[^1198]: The prosomoia stichera by St. Theodore the Studite at Wednesday Vespers in Tone 5 track Christ's physical journey from beyond the Jordan towards Bethany, announcing to the apostles that Lazarus is dead and that He goes to conquer death.

[^1199]: St. Theodore's sticheron in Tone 6 marks the second day of Lazarus in the grave: "Lazarus passes his second day in the tomb" (Двоедневствуетъ Лазарь во гробѣ), describing his vision of the departed from all ages held in the bonds of hades.

[^1200]: Reading from Genesis 43:26–31 and 45:1 at Wednesday Vespers, prefiguring the revelation of Christ unto His brethren. The heading in the Stauropegion edition contains an epigraphic misprint, reading Chapter 33 ("Глава̀ л҃г") instead of Chapter 43 ("м҃г").

[^1201]: The conclusion of the reading from Genesis (45:1–16) at Wednesday Vespers recounts the dramatic self-revelation of Joseph to his brethren in Egypt and his invitation for Jacob and his entire household to dwell in Goshen.

[^1202]: Psalm 115:5, 1 LXX (116:14, 10 MT), appointed as the second prokimenon of Wednesday Vespers of Palm Week, celebrating thanksgiving and redemption.

[^1203]: Reading from Proverbs 21:23–31 and 22:1–4 at Wednesday Vespers, contrasting divine wisdom, upright speech, and true riches in the fear of the Lord with arrogance and sloth.

[^1204]: Sessional hymn by St. Joseph the Hymnographer following the second stichology at Thursday Matins in Tone 5, urging the faithful to yoke contemplation and action in preparation to greet Christ.

[^1205]: Sessional hymn by St. Theodore the Studite following the third stichology at Thursday Matins in Tone 6, marking Lazarus's second day in the grave.

[^1212]: The Matins Aposticha Idiomelon of Thursday of Palm Week in Tone 5 combines allusions to Abraham entertaining the angels (Gen. 18:1–8; Heb. 13:2) with the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matt. 25:31–46), calling for fasting and almsgiving in order to be placed on Christ's right hand.

[^1213]: Theotokion at the Matins Aposticha on Thursday of Palm Week, modeled after the similar Marian hymns of supplication.

[^1214]: The Sixth Hour on Thursday of Palm Week appoints the Troparion of the Prophecy in Tone 1, with prokeimena from Psalms 117 and 118 LXX and the reading from Isaiah 65:8–16.

[^1215]: Psalm 117:20, 1 LXX (118:20, 1 MT), chanted before the Sixth Hour prophecy, foreshadowing Christ's triumphal entry through the gates of Jerusalem on Palm Sunday.

[^1216]: Reading from the Prophecy of Isaiah (65:8–16) at the Sixth Hour of Thursday: the Lord promises the preservation of a faithful remnant while condemning idolaters who set tables for demons, declaring that His servants shall eat, drink, and rejoice under a new name.

[^1217]: Psalm 118:32, 33 LXX (119:32, 33 MT), chanted as the second prokimenon of the Sixth Hour on Thursday of Palm Week.

[^1218]: Stichera prosomoia by St. Joseph the Hymnographer at Thursday Vespers in Tone 4, depicting the two disciples sent by Christ to find the colt (Matt. 21:1–7; Mark 11:1–7).

[^1219]: Sticheron prosomoion by St. Theodore the Studite at Thursday Vespers in Tone 8, contrasting Christ's celestial enthronement upon the Seraphim with His humble entry into Jerusalem upon a foal.

[^1220]: Psalm 119:1, 2 LXX (120:1, 2 MT), the first Gradual Psalm (Song of Ascents), appointed as the first prokimenon of Thursday Vespers of Palm Week.

[^1221]: Reading from Genesis 46:1–7 appointed across Thursday Vespers (fol. 443–444 / physical leaves p447–p448): God encourages Jacob at Beersheba ("the well of the oath"), promising to accompany him into Egypt and multiply his descendants.

[^1222]: Psalm 120:7, 1 LXX (121:7, 1 MT), the second Gradual Psalm, appointed as the second prokimenon of Thursday Vespers of Palm Week.

[^1223]: Reading from Proverbs 23:15–35 and 24:1–5 at Thursday Vespers, warning against drunkenness, lust, and evil companions while praising filial piety and divine wisdom.

[^1224]: The Thursday Vespers Aposticha Idiomelon in Tone 8 resumes the central Lenten and Palm Week typology of the Parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), praying for deliverance from the hard-heartedness of the rich man.

[^1225]: Cross-Theotokion at Thursday Vespers Aposticha, contemplating the grief of the Mother of God at the crucifixion of her Son.

[^1226]: Sessional hymn by St. Joseph the Hymnographer after the second stichology at Friday Matins in Tone 4, meditating on the sending of the two disciples to fetch the colt.

[^1227]: Sessional hymn by St. Theodore the Studite after the third stichology at Friday Matins in Tone 8, anticipating the overthrow of death by the raising of Lazarus.

[^1374]: Dogmatic Theotokion of Tone 1, sung at Saturday Vespers; cf. Ephesians 2:14: "Who hath made both one, and hath broken down the middle wall of partition between us"; John 16:33.

[^1375]: Supplementary Oktoechos stichera for Tone 2 at Friday Vespers, completing the Tone 1 supplement printed on leaf p500.

[^1376]: Celebrated Tone 2 funeral idiomelon by St. John of Damascus from the Order of Burial of the Departed.

[^1377]: Dogmatic Theotokion of Tone 2; cf. Exodus 3:2–3 (the Burning Bush on Mount Horeb), Exodus 13:21 (the pillar of fire), and Malachi 4:2 (the Sun of Righteousness).

[^1378]: The unabridged *Life of St. Mary of Egypt* attributed to St. Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem (c. 560–638 AD; PG 87:3697–3726), appointed by the Typikon to be read in two parts during Matins of Thursday of the Fifth Week of Great Lent (the Service of the Great Canon).

[^1379]: Tobit 12:7: "It is good to keep close the secret of a king, but it is honorable to reveal the works of God."

[^1380]: Matthew 25:24–30: The Parable of the Talents and the slothful servant who hid his Lord's silver in the earth.

[^1381]: St. Sophronius distinguishes the orthodox Palestinian ascetic Abba Zosimas from a heterodox monk of the same name known in sixth-century Palestine.

[^1382]: Genesis 12:1: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will show thee."

[^1383]: Psalm 26:1 (LXX) [Psalm 27:1 Masoretic]: "The Lord is my light and my Savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"

[^1384]: Palm Sunday (the Sunday of the Palm-Bearers, six days before Pascha), when the monks of the Jordanian lavra returned from their solitary Lenten desert sojourn.

[^1385]: Acknowledgment of Abba Zosimas's priestly ordination and liturgical service at the holy altar, revealed to St. Mary through the charismatic gift of clairvoyance (*diorasis*).

[^1386]: Ironical reversal of Acts 9:15 ("a chosen vessel"), confessing how in her youth she had made herself an instrument of the adversary before her repentance.

[^1387]: Ezekiel 18:23, 33:11; 2 Peter 3:9: God desires not the death of the sinner, but patiently awaits his conversion and life.

[^1388]: The Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-giving Cross, celebrated annually in Jerusalem on September 14 following the Dedication of the Church of the Resurrection.

[^1389]: Matthew 9:13; Luke 5:32; 1 Timothy 1:15: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners."

[^1390]: Echoing Psalm 94:11 (LXX) [Psalm 95:11 Masoretic] and Hebrews 3:11, 4:1–11, where crossing the Jordan signifies entering into the promised spiritual rest.

[^1391]: The ancient Monastery of St. John the Forerunner near the traditional site of the Lord's Baptism on the banks of the Jordan River.

[^1392]: Psalm 54:8–9 (LXX) [Psalm 55:7–8 Masoretic]: "Lo, I have fled afar off, and have abode in the wilderness. I waited for God Who saves me from faintheartedness and from tempest."

[^1393]: Numbers 11:5: "We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt freely... and our soul is dried away."

[^1394]: Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4 ("Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God"); Job 24:8 ("They embrace the rock for want of a shelter").

[^1395]: Psalm 71:18 (LXX) [Psalm 72:18 Masoretic]; Psalm 135:4 (LXX) [Psalm 136:4 Masoretic]: "Blessed be the Lord God, Who alone does marvelous things."

[^1396]: Holy and Great Thursday, commemorating the institution of the Mystical Supper of the Lord.

[^1397]: Acts 20:28: "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Spirit hath made you overseers."

[^1398]: Classical patristic maxim on *theosis* (deification through purification of heart), shared by St. Gregory the Theologian and St. Maximus the Confessor; cf. Matthew 5:8, 1 John 3:2–3.

[^1399]: Luke 2:29–30: The Canticle of St. Simeon the God-Receiver (*Nunc Dimittis*).

[^1400]: Hebrews 11:38: "(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth."

[^1401]: Genesis 3:19 ("for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return"). The Egyptian month of Pharmouthi 1 corresponds to April 1 in the Julian calendar, the traditional liturgical commemoration day of St. Mary of Egypt.

[^1402]: The *Beneficial Tale Concerning the Akathist* (*Diegesis ophelimos*), the historical synaxarion recounting the miraculous deliverances of Constantinople in 626, 674–678, and 717–718 AD through the intercession of the Most Holy Theotokos, appointed for Matins of the Saturday of the Fifth Week of Great Lent.

[^1403]: Emperor Heraclius (r. 610–641 AD), who deposed the usurper Phocas (r. 602–610 AD), and the Sassanid Persian King Khosrow II (Chosroes, r. 590–628 AD), whose general Shahrbaraz ("Sarbar") encamped at Chalcedon opposite Constantinople in 626 AD.

[^1404]: *Monoxyla* (Greek *monoxyla*, "single-timbered"): dugout vessels hollowed from single tree trunks used by the Slavic and Avar auxiliaries of the Khagan during the naval assault on the Golden Horn in August 626 AD.

[^1405]: Joshua 8:2–8 (the stratagem commanded by God at Ai); Judges 7:16–20 (Gideon's three hundred men with pitchers and torches routing the Midianites).

[^1406]: Psalm 67:2–3 (LXX) [Psalm 68:1–2 Masoretic]: "Let God arise, and let His enemies be scattered; and let them that hate Him flee from before His face. As smoke vanishes, so let them vanish; as wax melts before the fire."

[^1407]: The Sanctuary of the *Pege* (the Life-giving Spring, *Zoodochos Pege*), located outside the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople, where the imperial garrison routed an advance party of the besieging forces.

[^1408]: Psalm 78:10, 113:10 (LXX) ("Therefore should the heathen say, Where is their God?"); Proverbs 3:34 (LXX); James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5 ("God resists the proud, but gives grace unto the humble").

[^1409]: The Church of the Most Holy Theotokos at Blachernae on the shore of the Golden Horn (*Keras*), where the Avar-Slavic fleet of *monoxyla* was miraculously sunk by a sudden tempest on August 7, 626 AD; cf. Exodus 14:21–28 (the drowning of Pharaoh's army in the Red Sea).

[^1410]: Exodus 15:6–7 (LXX): "Thy right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength; Thy right hand, O Lord, hath broken the enemies; and in the multitude of Thy glory Thou hast crushed the adversaries."

[^1411]: The classical etiological explanation for the Greek name *Akathistos* (*Ἀκάθιστος*, "not-sitting"): the clergy, monastics, and people of Constantinople remained standing throughout the whole-night vigil of thanksgiving for the deliverance of the Queen of Cities in August 626 AD.

[^1412]: The Second Arab Siege of Constantinople (674–678 AD) under the Umayyad Caliph Mu'awiya I and Emperor Constantine IV Pogonatos ("the Bearded", r. 668–685 AD). The Slavonic term *Roistolom* reflects the Byzantine Greek *Rhodostolos* (literally "commander of the fleet" or "Rhodes-expedition commander"). The surviving Arab fleet was wrecked by a severe storm off the coast of Syllaeum in Pamphylia.

[^1413]: The Third Arab Siege of Constantinople (717–718 AD) under Caliph Sulayman / Umar II and general Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik, during the reign of Emperor Leo III the Isaurian (r. 717–741 AD). The chroniclers record an invading fleet of 1,800 vessels.

[^1414]: Psalm 82:2–5 (LXX) [Psalm 83:1–4 Masoretic]: "O God, who shall be like unto Thee? Hold not Thy peace, and be not still, O God. For lo, Thine enemies have made a noise; and they that hate Thee have lifted up their head... They have said, Come, and let us destroy them from being a nation"; and Philippians 2:11: "And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father."

[^1415]: Emperor Leo III formed an alliance with Khan Tervel of Bulgaria, whose armies assaulted the Arab land forces besieging Constantinople in 718 AD, inflicting over 20,000 casualties and forcing the lifting of the land siege.

[^1416]: The great defensive iron chain stretched across the Golden Horn between the walls of Constantinople and the Fortress of Galata (Kastellion), preventing hostile naval vessels from penetrating the harbor; Byzantine ships equipped with siphon tubes projector-discharged "Greek Fire" (*liquid fire*, invented by Kallinikos of Heliopolis), setting the Arab ships ablaze.

[^1417]: During the harsh winter of 717–718 AD, snow covered the ground for over a hundred days, cutting off Arab supply lines and causing devastating famine and pestilence among the besiegers, forcing many to desert or surrender to the Byzantine forces.

[^1418]: In the autumn of 718 AD, as the remnant of the Arab fleet attempted to sail through the Aegean Sea, an undersea volcanic eruption and tempest near Thera (Santorini) superheated the sea waters and showered the vessels with burning pumice and hail, boiling the pitch and sinking virtually the entire fleet, with only five (in this Slavonic account, three) vessels surviving to reach Syria.

[^1419]: Psalm 73:13 (LXX) [Psalm 74:13 Masoretic]: "Thou didst divide the sea by Thy strength; Thou didst crush the heads of the dragons in the water"; and Exodus 15:1: "Let us sing unto the Lord, for He is gloriously glorified: the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea."

[^1420]: Romans 12:9 ("Let love be without hypocrisy"); 1 Timothy 1:5; Galatians 5:22–23; Ephesians 4:1–6. St. John Chrysostom and early Christian commentators frequently emphasize that internal virtuous living and love without hypocrisy constitute spiritual instruments far more pleasing to God than musical instruments and vocal praise alone.

[^1421]: A classical Byzantine homiletic and rhetorical metaphor, likening the end of a long sermon or panegyric to a vessel lowering its sails and entering the calm haven of silence after traversing a vast ocean of divine wonders.

[^1422]: The *Markian Chapters* (*Главы́ Ма́рковы*, *Kaphalaia tou Markou*), attributed to Hieromonk Mark of the Monastery of St. Sabas or Bishop Mark of Otranto, provide precise combinatorial rubrics for resolving coincidences between immovable feasts of the Menaion and movable liturgical days of the Triodion and Pentecostarion.

[^1423]: The Feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs (St. Basil the Great, St. Gregory the Theologian, and St. John Chrysostom, January 30) coinciding with the Sundays of the Publican and Pharisee, the Prodigal Son, or Meatfare Sunday. The rubrics refer to the order prescribed for the First and Second Findings of the Precious Head of St. John the Baptist (February 24).

[^1424]: Rubrics for the Forefeast of the Meeting of the Lord (February 1) when it falls on the Sunday of the Publican and Pharisee, the Prodigal Son, Meatfare Sunday, or Cheesefare Sunday.

[^1425]: Meatfare Saturday is dedicated universally to the commemoration of all departed Orthodox Christians (Saturday of Souls), while Cheesefare Saturday commemorates all the holy ascetic fathers and mothers who shone forth in the monastic life.

[^1426]: Rubrics for the Great Feast of the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*, February 2) coinciding with the Pre-Lenten Sundays (Publican and Pharisee, Prodigal Son, Meatfare, or Cheesefare).

[^1427]: An important liturgical provision of the Sabbaite and Ruthenian Typika: when the Great Feast of the Meeting of the Lord coincides with a Pre-Lenten Sunday, the praises (*lauds*) stichera of the Triodion are transferred to the Litiya at Vespers on Saturday evening so that none of the appointed Sunday Triodion hymnography is omitted.

[^1428]: Because a Great Feast of the Lord cannot admit funeral commemorations, when the Meeting of the Lord falls on Meatfare Saturday, the entire universal Memorial Service for the Departed is transferred either to the preceding Saturday or to the preceding Thursday of Meatfare Week.

[^1429]: The Afterfeast (*Poprazdnstvo*) of the Meeting of the Lord, encompassing the days following February 2 during which the festal hymns continue to be sung alongside the daily services of the Octoechos, Menaion, and Triodion.

[^1430]: The Apodosis (*Otdanie*, Greek *Apodosis*) of the Meeting of the Lord: according to the Typikon, the apodosis cannot be celebrated on Meatfare Sunday or during Clean Week; its celebration is therefore adjusted according to the day of the week on which the feast falls, concluding at the latest on Cheesefare Sunday.

[^1431]: The First and Second Findings of the Precious Head of the Holy Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John (*Честно́е ѡ҆брѣ́тенїе честны́ѧ Главы̀ І҆ѡа́нна Предте́чи*), celebrated on February 24. These Markian chapters govern the complex liturgical intersections that occur when February 24 coincides with the movable cycle of the Pre-Lenten period and Great Lent, ranging from Meatfare Wednesday through the Tuesday of the First Week of the Great Fast, and subsequent Lenten weekdays and Sundays.

[^1432]: Meatfare Saturday is dedicated universally to the general commemoration of all departed Orthodox Christians (the Universal Memorial Saturday of Souls, *Сꙋббѡ́та мѧсопꙋ́стнаѧ ᲂу҆со́пшихъ*). Because the solemn ancestral requiem office cannot be displaced or easily combined with a joyous saintly festival of Polyeleos rank, the feast of the Forerunner is transferred in its entirety to the preceding Friday.

[^1433]: On Monday and Tuesday of Cheesefare Week, although the strict dietary transition has begun (meat is excluded, but dairy and eggs are permitted throughout), the liturgical order remains festive, permitting the celebration of the Polyeleos, Great Doxology, and the readings of the Forerunner alongside the movable Triodion hymnography.

[^1434]: On Wednesday and Friday of Cheesefare Week, the services already assume an aliturgical, penitential character: prostrations are appointed, the Prayer of St. Ephrem is recited, and the Divine Liturgy is not celebrated. Consequently, the festal celebration of the Forerunner cannot be held on these days and is transferred to Tuesday or Thursday respectively.

[^1435]: On Cheesefare Thursday, because the eve of the day (Wednesday afternoon) contains Lenten elements, Vespers is served after the Ninth Hour and the Prayer of St. Ephrem, with readings and Great Prokeimena. At the monastic refectory, a dispensation for cheese and eggs is granted in honor of the feast.

[^1436]: On Cheesefare Saturday, the Church commemorates all the Holy Ascetic Fathers and Mothers who shone forth in the monastic life (*Па́мѧть всѣ́хъ прпⷣбныхъ ѻ҆тє́цъ въ по́двизѣ провозсїя́вшихъ*). When the Finding of the Head of the Forerunner coincides with this day, the hymnography of the Ascetic Fathers is harmonized with that of the Forerunner.

[^1437]: Pure Monday (*Чи́стый понедѣ́льникъ*), the opening day of Clean Week and of the Great Fast, is kept with the strictest fasting and mournful penitence; no festal celebration is permitted. The entire service of the Forerunner is therefore transferred backward to Cheesefare Sunday.

[^1438]: When the feast falls on any weekday of Clean Week (Tuesday through Friday), the penitential services of the Great Canon of St. Andrew of Crete cannot be displaced; the festal service of the Forerunner is transferred either backward to Cheesefare Sunday or forward to the First Saturday of Lent (commemoration of the Miracle of the Kolyva of the Great Martyr Theodore the Tyro).

[^1439]: The Provincial Synod of Lviv (*Synodus Provincialis Ruthenorum Galiciae*), convened under Metropolitan Sylvester Cardinal Sembratovych in 1891 (Slavonic year `҂аѡч҃а` = 1891 AD), which codified and standardized liturgical practices across the Greek Catholic Metropolitanate of Kyiv-Halych and the Archeparchy of Lviv, resolving local rubrical adaptations, here sanctioning Small Compline instead of Great Compline.

[^1440]: The First Sunday of Great Lent (Sunday of the Triumph of Orthodoxy, *Недѣ́лѧ правосла́вїѧ*). The service of the Forerunner is combined with that of the Triumph of Orthodoxy following the rubrics prescribed for the Third Sunday of Lent (Veneration of the Cross), omitting only the ceremony of the veneration of the Cross.

[^1441]: When the Finding of the Head of the Forerunner falls on Monday of the Second, Third, or Fourth Weeks of Great Lent, Great Vespers with the Great Prokeimenon is served on Sunday evening, followed by Matins with Polyeleos and the celebration of the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts on Monday.

[^1442]: An exceptional rubrical contingency: when, due to grave necessity or the absence of a priest authorized to serve the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts on a major feast with Polyeleos, the Presanctified Liturgy cannot be celebrated, the Typika (with Typika Psalms, Beatitudes, and festal Epistle and Gospel) are chanted in place of the Liturgy.

[^1443]: The *paraecclesiarch* (*параекклисїа́рхъ* / church warden / candle-lighter) tolls two bells (*зна́менаетъ къ два̀ кампа́на*) to signal the monastic assembly's transition from the Typika to Great Lenten Vespers.

[^1444]: St. Tarasios, Patriarch of Constantinople (commemorated February 25), defender of the holy icons at the Seventh Ecumenical Council (Nicaea II, 787 AD), whose commemoration immediately follows the Finding of the Head of the Forerunner (February 24).

[^1445]: When the Finding of the Head of the Forerunner occurs on an ordinary fasting weekday of the Second, Third, or Fourth Weeks of Lent, Vespers is united with the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts in the afternoon, or served standalone without the Liturgy if none is celebrated.

[^1446]: On the Second or Third Saturday of Great Lent (traditionally appointed as ancestral memorial Saturdays of Souls), the celebration of the Finding of the Head of the Forerunner displaces the requiem service and is combined with the hymns of the Octoechos and the Triodion.

[^1447]: The Second Sunday of Great Lent (commemoration of St. Gregory Palamas, Archbishop of Thessalonica). The Sunday Resurrectional service is combined with the hymns of the Triodion and the Forerunner, with Polyeleos, Magnification, and the Great Doxology.

[^1448]: The Third Sunday of Great Lent (Sunday of the Veneration of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross, *Недѣ́лѧ крⷭ҇топокло́ннаѧ*). The service harmonizes the Resurrectional hymns, the veneration and hymns of the Precious Cross, and the feast of the Forerunner.

[^1449]: The Holy Forty Martyrs of Sebaste (*Святи́и четыре́десѧть му́чєницы въ Севасті́йстѣмъ є҆́зерѣ му́чєнически сконча́вшїисѧ*), commemorated on March 9. When March 9 falls on the First, Second, Third, or Fourth Saturdays of Great Lent, the order of services follows precisely the rubrics established for the Finding of the Head of the Forerunner.

[^1450]: On Wednesday of the Fourth Week of Lent (Mid-Lent / Wednesday of the Cross), the commemoration of the Forty Martyrs is transferred backward to Tuesday, because Wednesday is dedicated pre-eminently to the Veneration of the Precious Cross.

[^1451]: On Thursday of the Great Canon (Fifth Week), the Forty Martyrs are transferred backward to Tuesday of that week because the entire Thursday office is occupied by the Great Canon of St. Andrew of Crete and the Life of St. Mary of Egypt.

[^1452]: On the Saturday of the Akathist (Fifth Saturday of Great Lent), the Forty Martyrs are transferred to the Fifth Sunday of the Fast, so that the festive Akathist Hymn to the Mother of God may be sung without curtailment.

[^1453]: The Forefeast of the Annunciation of the Most Holy Theotokos (March 24) coinciding with weekdays of Great Lent (Monday through Friday), combining the forefestal hymnography with the Lenten Triodion at Vespers and the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts.

[^1454]: Forefeast of the Annunciation coinciding with the Third or Fourth Saturday of Great Lent. A celebratory chime of two small bells (*трезво́нъ въ дво́и ма́лыѧ колокола̀*) is sounded, and the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts is celebrated on Friday evening.

[^1455]: Forefeast of the Annunciation on the Third Sunday of Lent (Veneration of the Cross). The hymnography of the Precious Cross is joined with the Resurrection and Forefeast, taking precedence over the daily Triodion commemorations.

[^1456]: Forefeast of the Annunciation on Mid-Lent Wednesday (Cross-Veneration Wednesday). Prostrations are made at all services, the Cross is venerated at the First Hour, and the Triodion cross hymnography takes prominence alongside the forefestal stichera and canon.

[^1457]: Forefeast of the Annunciation on Thursday of the Fourth Week of Great Lent. The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts is celebrated on Wednesday evening, followed by the combined forefestal and Triodion office on Thursday morning.

[^1458]: Forefeast of the Annunciation on the Fourth or Fifth Sunday of Great Lent. The customary secondary commemorations of St. John Climacus (Fourth Sunday) or St. Mary of Egypt (Fifth Sunday) are postponed or transferred to another day at the discretion of the ecclesiarch.

[^1459]: Forefeast of the Annunciation coinciding with the Fifth Saturday of Great Lent (Saturday of the Akathist), combining the Akathist hymnography with that of the forefeast.

[^1460]: Forefeast of the Annunciation on Lazarus Saturday. The forefestal service is transferred to Great and Holy Thursday because Lazarus Saturday is dedicated exclusively to the Raising of Lazarus by the Lord.

[^1461]: The comprehensive Markian Chapters governing the Feast of the Annunciation of the Most Holy Theotokos (March 25) coinciding with the movable cycles of Great Lent, Lazarus Saturday, Palm Sunday, Passion Week, Holy Pascha, and Bright Week. In the Ruthenian Typikon, the movable date of the Annunciation can range from Thursday of the Third Week of Lent to Wednesday of Bright Week.

[^1462]: The general order of Old Testament readings for the Annunciation when it falls on a Saturday or Sunday of Lent: five festal Old Testament readings are appointed (three at Vespers and two at the Liturgy, or all five at Great Vespers on the eve of Saturday/Sunday).

[^1463]: An ancient monastic procession (*лїті́а*) outside the monastery walls with crosses and banners, conducted at the Third Hour of the day on the Annunciation.

[^1464]: St. John Chrysostom's renowned festive homily for the Annunciation of the Theotokos, beginning *"Again the joy of the Annunciation..."* (*Πάλιν χαρᾶς εὐαγγέλια* / *Па́ки ра́дость Бл҃говѣ́щенїа*).

[^1465]: Psalm 103:4 (LXX) [Psalm 104:4 Masoretic]: "Who makes His angels spirits, and His ministers a flame of fire"; and Hebrews 1:7.

[^1466]: Hebrews 2:11–18 (Pericope 306): "For both He that sanctifies and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause He is not ashamed to call them brethren..."

[^1467]: Psalm 71:6, 17 (LXX) [Psalm 72:6, 17 Masoretic]: "He shall come down like rain upon the fleece; and as drops falling upon the earth... His name shall be blessed unto ages."

[^1468]: Luke 1:24–38 (Pericope 3): The Conception of St. Elizabeth and the Annunciation of the Archangel Gabriel to the Most Holy Theotokos.

[^1469]: Psalm 131:13 (LXX) [Psalm 132:13 Masoretic]: "For the Lord hath chosen Zion; He hath desired it for His habitation."

[^1470]: An authoritative canonical and rubrical decree attributed to St. John the Faster (*Ioannes Nesteutes*), Patriarch of Constantinople (582–595 AD), defending the celebration of the full Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom and the dispensation for fish on the Annunciation during Great Lent, and forbidding penitential laments such as *"Let my prayer be set forth"* (*Да испра́вится моли́тва моя̀*) when the full Liturgy is served.

[^1471]: Rubrics for when, due to grave pastoral necessity or lack of a priest, the Divine Liturgy cannot be celebrated on the Annunciation; fish and wine are still permitted at the monastic table once during the day.

[^1472]: The Synaxis of the Archangel Gabriel (*Собо́ръ ст҃а́гѡ а҆рха́ггела Гаврїи́ла*), commemorated on March 26, the day following the Annunciation.

[^1473]: Annunciation coinciding with the Third or Fourth Saturday of Great Lent. On Friday evening, the Presanctified Liturgy is combined with Vespers of the Annunciation, and Great Compline is chanted at the first hour of the night.

[^1474]: Annunciation on the Third Sunday of Great Lent (Sunday of the Veneration of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross). The Divine Liturgy of St. Basil the Great is celebrated with the Hymn to the Cross (*"Before Thy Cross we bow down, O Master..."*) in place of the Trisagion.

[^1475]: An inviolable rubrical rule of the Byzantine and Ruthenian Typika: whenever the Annunciation falls on any weekday of Great Lent, the Divine Liturgy of St. Basil the Great is celebrated without exception (*быва́етъ Літургі́а вели́кагѡ Васїлїа непосмѣ́ннѡ*), united with Vespers on fasting days, or in its regular order on Saturday and Sunday.

[^1476]: Annunciation on Monday of the Second, Third, or Sixth (Palm) Weeks of Great Lent.

[^1477]: Annunciation on Mid-Lent Wednesday (Cross-Veneration Wednesday). The stichera, Doxastica, and canon of the Cross are postponed to Monday or Friday of that same week, while the Annunciation with the Triodion Mid-Lent triode is celebrated on Wednesday; veneration of the Cross takes place at the First Hour.

[^1478]: Annunciation on the Fourth or Fifth Sunday of Great Lent.

[^1479]: When the Annunciation falls on Wednesday of the Fifth Week of Great Lent, the Great Penitential Canon of St. Andrew of Crete (ordinarily appointed for Thursday Matins of the Fifth Week) is transferred backward to Tuesday Matins of that same week. Because Wednesday is the festal day of the Annunciation, kathisma readings and prostrations are suspended, and the Apodosis of the feast is celebrated on Thursday; thus the Great Canon cannot be sung on Thursday and is anticipated on Tuesday.

[^1480]: When the Annunciation falls on Thursday of the Fifth Week of Great Lent—the appointed day of the Great Canon of St. Andrew of Crete—the Great Canon is likewise transferred to Tuesday of that week and chanted with the Tuesday triode. On Thursday itself, the festal office of the Annunciation is celebrated, united with the apostolic triode from the Triodion.

[^1481]: When the Annunciation falls on Friday of the Fifth Week of Great Lent, the Forefeast of the Annunciation (ordinarily kept on Thursday, March 24) is transferred backward to Wednesday, because Thursday is fully occupied by the celebration of the Great Canon.

[^1482]: The concurrence of the Annunciation (March 25) with the Saturday of the Akathist (the Fifth Saturday of Great Lent). This creates a magnificent liturgical synthesis of the two paramount Byzantine celebrations of the Mother of God, uniting the four strophes of the Akathist Hymn with the festal Annunciation hymnography at Compline, Matins, and the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom.

[^1483]: The four-ode canon (*Четверопѣ́снецъ*) of the Triodion for the Saturday of the Akathist, composed by St. Joseph the Hymnographer (Odes 6, 7, 8, and 9). Because the Matins of the combined feast is already exceptionally dense with the full Akathist and the Annunciation canon, this triode/tetrode is transferred to Thursday Compline.

[^1484]: The descent (*схо́дъ* / *katabasis* / gathering into the center of the nave): The liturgical rubrics direct both choirs to descend from their respective kliros stalls and assemble together in the middle of the nave to solemnly chant the Ninth Heirmos (*"As the living ark of God..."*) and make a unified prostration.

[^1485]: The concluding colophon of the 1906 Lviv Stauropegion Lenten Triodion: *Коне́цъ и҆ Бг҃ꙋ Сла́ва* ("The End, and to God be the Glory"), printed on page 528 (physical leaf 532) beneath a decorative woodcut tailpiece. This marks the complete conclusion of the entire monument, issued by the Stauropegion Institute of Lviv under the archpastoral blessing of Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky of Halych, Bishop Hryhoriy Chekhovych of Peremyshl, and Bishop Hryhoriy Khomyshyn of Stanyslaviv.
